Take-home Exercise 3: Technical Report

  • Show All Code

Station choice under the Jurong Region and Cross Island Line Phase 1 scenarios

Author

Davin Cuaso

Published

31 October 2026

Modified

31 October 2026

Submission hub · Executive summary · Project source

1 Overview

The question is whether adding the Jurong Region Line (JRL) and the first phase of the Cross Island Line (CRL1) changes where rail users are likely to board and alight. A station does not draw passengers from a fixed circle. Travellers can choose among several stations, and the choice depends on the station’s setting and on the cost of reaching it. I use a probabilistic station-choice model for that comparison, with separate current and proposed networks.

This report currently has two different levels of evidence. The station and land-use analysis is complete and uses recorded public geographic layers. The ridership model is implemented but has not been calibrated, because the LTA origin–destination (OD) trip file is not in the course repository or the supplied workspace. I do not report trip estimates from a substitute or simulated OD table. The result sections identify exactly what the missing file will unlock.

The official brief calls for two interaction frames, origin market potential, destination observed ridership and attraction measures, calibration, validation, future-station prediction, and a comparison of existing station market areas. The project is organised around those outputs.

2 Study questions and units

  1. How many distinct station locations are in the current and proposed networks?
  2. Which HDB blocks gain straight-line proximity to rail under the proposed network?
  3. Once observed OD counts are available, how well can a model using local activity, connectivity and distance reproduce station-level tap-outs?
  4. Holding the observed origin market fixed, which destinations could gain or lose share when proposed stations enter the choice set?

The model’s unit will be a directed origin–destination station pair for one LTA data month, restricted to the WEEKDAY day type. Station-level ridership means recorded destination tap-outs summed across those pairs. In the geographic audit, a “station” is one physical location; the line codes of an interchange are grouped under one station name.

3 Data sources and their roles

Show the R code 
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Source = c("Operational and future station coordinates", "HDB Existing Building",
             "LTA Bus Stop", "Master Plan 2025 Land Use Layer",
             "LTA train OD passenger volume"),
  Snapshot = c("Repository snapshot, 31 Oct 2026", "Buildings dated Nov 2025",
               "Downloaded 31 Oct 2026", "Gazetted Dec 2025",
               "Awaiting a monthly CSV or ZIP"),
  Role = c("Station locations and scenario codes", "Residential-building count and proximity",
           "Bus-stop poles near proposed stations", "Mapped activity area near destinations",
           "Observed weekday station-to-station trips")
), col.names = c("Dataset", "Time reference", "Use"))
Dataset Time reference Use
Operational and future station coordinates Repository snapshot, 31 Oct 2026 Station locations and scenario codes
HDB Existing Building Buildings dated Nov 2025 Residential-building count and proximity
LTA Bus Stop Downloaded 31 Oct 2026 Bus-stop poles near proposed stations
Master Plan 2025 Land Use Layer Gazetted Dec 2025 Mapped activity area near destinations
LTA train OD passenger volume Awaiting a monthly CSV or ZIP Observed weekday station-to-station trips

The station coordinate repository derives most points from URA or LTA records and flags manual estimates in a source field. I saved its operational and future CSVs with the project so the scenario cannot silently change when that repository is updated. The brief’s direct LTA Train Station ZIP returned HTTP 403 when checked on 31 October, so the saved compilation remains the coordinate source. HDB Existing Building, LTA Bus Stop, and the Master Plan 2025 Land Use Layer are downloaded directly from data.gov.sg by R/prepare_geography.R; the raw GeoJSON files stay in an ignored local cache. Derived tables and figures are in results/ and figures/.

These choices cover four of the brief’s six recommended data roles: current station locations, future locations, HDB buildings and bus stops. The fifth, LTA train OD passenger volume, is specified in the model but still needs an Account Key and a genuine monthly extract. The sixth, OpenStreetMap POIs via Geofabrik, was considered but not added: the Master Plan layer gives a consistent island-wide zoning measure for this first model, while POI tagging and completeness vary by place. That decision does not make zoning a count of jobs or visits.

The LTA OD Train endpoint requires a DataMall Account Key. Its user guide defines YEAR_MONTH, DAY_TYPE, TIME_PER_HOUR, origin and destination station codes, and TOTAL_TRIPS. The code accepts LTA’s CSV or ZIP once obtained. The report will state the exact data month after ingestion; no month is assumed in advance.

4 Preparing the station scenarios

The current CSV has 213 line-code records. Grouping records with the same physical station name gives 181 existing station locations. For the proposed scenario I retain JS1–JS12, JW1–JW5, and JE1–JE7 (24 JRL codes) plus CR2–CR13 (12 CRL1 codes). This matches the assignment’s 24 plus 12 scope and LTA’s CRL1 phase description. The extra JS2A Forest Hill record in the future coordinate file is excluded from this fixed 24-code JRL scenario. CRL Phase 2 and its Punggol extension are also excluded because they are outside CRL1.

Seven proposed codes refer to existing interchange locations: Choa Chu Kang, Boon Lay, Jurong East, Pasir Ris, Hougang, Ang Mo Kio and Bright Hill. They add a line connection but not another destination point. The result is 29 new physical locations, giving 210 existing-plus-proposed stations. Double-counting an interchange as two destinations would inflate its predicted share, so the station-name grouping matters.

Show the R code 
knitr::kable(coverage[1:3, ], col.names = c("Check", "Count"))
Check Count
Existing physical stations 181
New physical stations 29
HDB blocks in source 13436

The coordinates are converted from longitude and latitude (EPSG:4326) to SVY21 / Singapore TM (EPSG:3414) before distance calculations. In this projected system, the station-to-station and building-to-station distances are in metres. I validate missing coordinates, duplicate station codes, and the expected JRL/CRL1 code counts before any result is written.

5 Geographic measures before ridership calibration

5.1 Residential blocks within reach

I take the centroid of each completed HDB building polygon and find its nearest existing and proposed station. An 800 m threshold is a simple spatial screen: it asks whether a block’s mapped centre lies within 800 m in a straight line. The count is not a population estimate, because blocks differ in floor count and household size. It also does not measure an actual walking route.

Show the R code 
knitr::kable(coverage[4:6, ], col.names = c("Measure", "HDB blocks"))
Measure HDB blocks
4 HDB blocks within 800 m of existing rail 9645
5 HDB blocks newly within 800 m 1319
6 HDB blocks nearer to a new station 2110

Of 13,436 buildings, 9,645 are within 800 m of an existing physical station. The scenario adds 1,319 buildings to that threshold. A further 2,110 buildings are nearer to a proposed station than to any current one, whether or not they cross the 800 m line. These two figures answer different questions: new threshold coverage versus a shorter straight-line distance.

Show the R code 
knitr::include_graphics("figures/hdb-new-coverage.png")

The newly covered blocks are concentrated around planned stops in the west and north-east. The west contains much of the JRL extension’s residential catchment, while the eastern CRL1 stations add pockets around Pasir Ris East and Tampines North. This map is a geographic opportunity measure, not a forecast of journeys: some blocks may already reach rail by bus, and an apparently close station may require a longer walk around barriers.

Show the R code 
knitr::kable(line_coverage,
             col.names = c("Nearest proposed line", "Newly reached HDB blocks"))
Nearest proposed line Newly reached HDB blocks
CRL1 586
JRL 733

The line totals assign each newly reached building to its closest new station. They should not be read as a benefit–cost comparison of the two projects: the lines serve different places, and HDB buildings exclude private housing and many work destinations.

Show the R code 
knitr::include_graphics("figures/new-station-blocks.png")

Pasir Ris East has the largest count in this measure (216), followed by Serangoon North (151) and Tengah Plantation (144). The chart assigns each newly reached block to its nearest proposed station, so a block is counted once. It does not imply that these will be the busiest new stations. Business districts and interchange stations can draw riders from much farther away than the surrounding HDB blocks.

5.2 Sensitivity to the threshold

Show the R code 
knitr::kable(sensitivity, col.names = c("Radius (m)", "Existing blocks reached", "Newly reached blocks"))
Radius (m) Existing blocks reached Newly reached blocks
600 7395 1206
800 9645 1319
1000 11178 1106

The 800 m result is not a natural boundary. The table repeats the same centroid calculation at 600 m and 1,000 m. A larger radius includes more buildings but also accepts walks that may be unattractive or impossible in practice. The model itself uses continuous station-to-station distance rather than treating these circles as a rigid passenger market.

5.3 Destination activity proxy

For each station, I count HDB block centroids and sum the area of mapped commercial, business, civic, education, health, hotel and mixed-use parcels whose centroids fall within 800 m. The land-use layer records zoning, not occupied jobs or realised visits. A large parcel whose centre lies just inside the circle is counted in full, so the figure is an approximate activity proxy. The two measures are kept separate in the model: one describes nearby housing blocks; the other describes mapped non-residential opportunities.

Show the R code 
knitr::include_graphics("figures/proposed-activity.png")

The activity ranking differs from the HDB-block ranking. That is the reason to include both predictors: a station serving industrial or commercial land could attract destination trips even with few completed HDB blocks nearby. The chart does not tell us how many workers or visitors use those parcels.

5.4 Nearby bus stops

The LTA bus-stop layer has 5,205 unique stop codes. For each of the 29 new physical station locations, I count mapped stop poles within 400 m of the station point. This is a different check from the 800 m HDB building screen: it describes nearby bus infrastructure, not the number of residents or a catchment of passengers.

Show the R code 
knitr::include_graphics("figures/proposed-bus-stops.png")

Choa Chu Kang West has 16 mapped stops within 400 m; Pandan Reservoir and Serangoon North have 14 each. The complete station table includes all 29 locations. These counts cannot distinguish a busy transfer point from a group of lightly served roadside stops. Routes, headways, stop direction and walking connections would be needed before treating bus access as a behavioural predictor.

6 Interaction data and observed market potential

The model script constructs a full directed choice table rather than using only pairs that appear in the OD CSV. Zero-flow pairs must remain in the choice set; otherwise the denominator in a station-choice probability would be calculated from observed trips alone. A same-station trip is removed because its zero spatial distance is not meaningful for this interstation model. Distances use station points in SVY21; they are not rail travel times or network path lengths.

Show the R code 
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Table = c("Current interactions", "Proposed interactions", "Origins", "Destinations"),
  Key = c("origin + destination", "origin + destination", "origin", "destination"),
  Fields = c("observed trips, attraction, distance_km, probability",
             "attraction, distance_km, probability",
             "observed outbound weekday trips = market_potential",
             "observed inbound weekday trips, HDB blocks, activity area, line count")
), col.names = c("Data frame", "Join key", "Principal columns"))
Data frame Join key Principal columns
Current interactions origin + destination observed trips, attraction, distance_km, probability
Proposed interactions origin + destination attraction, distance_km, probability
Origins origin observed outbound weekday trips = market_potential
Destinations destination observed inbound weekday trips, HDB blocks, activity area, line count

LTA merges some interchange codes in the OD file (for example CC1-NE6-NS24). R/model.R splits these codes and maps their components to one physical station name. It saves unmatched codes and stops if they represent more than 5% of trip counts. The file must contain exactly one YEAR_MONTH, valid hourly values, and non-negative trips. Only WEEKDAY and TRAIN rows enter this version of the model. The origin total is a monthly aggregate across weekdays, not a per-day rate.

7 Calibration and validation

For an origin i and available destination j, the station-choice utility is

\[ U_{ij}=\beta_H\log(1+H_j)+\beta_A\log(1+A_j)+\beta_L\log(L_j)-\beta_D\log(d_{ij}+0.25), \qquad P_{ij}=\frac{\exp(U_{ij})}{\sum_{k\ne i}\exp(U_{ik})}. \]

Here \(H_j\) is HDB block count within 800 m, \(A_j\) is approximate activity hectares, \(L_j\) is the number of rail lines, and \(d_{ij}\) is straight-line distance in kilometres. The 0.25 km offset keeps the distance term finite at very short separations. The four coefficients are fitted by maximising the conditional multinomial likelihood of observed OD trips. The coefficient bounds enforce non-negative attraction effects and non-negative distance decay; a boundary estimate would warn that a predictor may add little information. These are modelling choices, not measured behavioural constants.

I reserve 20% of origin stations, selected with seed 626, before fitting. Their trip-weighted log loss is compared with a fitted distance-only model. The final coefficients are then refitted to all observed origins. For the current network, estimated destination tap-outs are the sum of each origin’s observed market potential multiplied by its destination probabilities. The code checks that probabilities sum to one per origin and that total estimated trips equal the observed trip total.

Show the R code 
if (has_model) {
  checks <- read.csv(file.path(model_dir, "checks.csv"))
  coefficients <- read.csv(file.path(model_dir, "coefficients.csv"))
  cat("The supplied OD file covers **", checks$month[1], "**. The model matched **",
      round(100 * checks$matched_trip_share[1], 1),
      "%** of weekday trips to the station coordinate table.\n\n", sep = "")
  print(knitr::kable(coefficients, digits = 3,
                     col.names = c("Model term", "Fitted coefficient")))
  cat("\nThe held-out log loss per trip is **", round(checks$heldout_logloss_per_trip[1], 3),
      "**, compared with **", round(checks$distance_only_logloss_per_trip[1], 3),
      "** for distance alone. The current-network station MAE is **",
      fmt(round(checks$station_mae[1])), "** monthly weekday tap-outs.\n", sep = "")
} else {
  cat("::: {.callout-warning title=\"Calibration pending\"}\n",
      "The LTA OD Train file has not been supplied. There are no fitted coefficients,",
      "validation scores or observed-versus-estimated station ridership values to report.\n:::\n")
}
WarningCalibration pending

The LTA OD Train file has not been supplied. There are no fitted coefficients, validation scores or observed-versus-estimated station ridership values to report.

8 Proposed-network comparison

The first counterfactual holds each existing origin’s observed outbound trip total fixed and adds the 29 distinct new station locations as possible destinations. Existing interchanges gain their proposed line connection. The fitted coefficients stay unchanged. This isolates a change in destination choice under the expanded set of stations. It does not estimate new trips generated by future housing, trips starting at new stations, or transfers inside paid rail areas. New-station figures from this scenario would be captured tap-outs from existing origins, not total future station ridership.

Show the R code 
if (has_model) {
  pred <- read.csv(file.path(model_dir, "station-predictions.csv"))
  top_new <- pred |>
    dplyr::filter(status == "Planned new") |>
    dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(estimated_scenario)) |>
    dplyr::select(destination, estimated_scenario) |>
    head(10)
  print(knitr::kable(top_new, digits = 0,
                     col.names = c("New destination", "Captured monthly weekday tap-outs")))
  existing_change <- pred |>
    dplyr::filter(status == "Existing") |>
    dplyr::arrange(change) |>
    dplyr::select(destination, change, change_pct) |>
    head(10)
  cat("\nThe largest modelled reductions among existing destination stations are:\n\n")
  print(knitr::kable(existing_change, digits = 1,
                     col.names = c("Existing station", "Trip change", "Change (%)")))
} else {
  cat("The comparison table will be populated from the LTA OD file. No future-station",
      "ridership or existing-station share change is claimed yet.\n")
}

The comparison table will be populated from the LTA OD file. No future-station ridership or existing-station share change is claimed yet.

The interaction outputs retain origin, destination, attraction, distance_km and probability for both networks. They can be inspected directly rather than relying on a map’s colour scale. Since the scenario conserves origin totals, gains at new destinations must be balanced by losses at existing destinations; this is a feature of this fixed-market scenario, not a statement that systemwide rail demand cannot grow.

9 Assumptions and limitations

The coordinate file is a secondary compilation and may not place every platform or entrance exactly where passengers enter. The JS2A omission follows the brief’s 24-code JRL scope rather than claiming the station is not planned. Station name grouping is suitable for physical locations, but it masks separate paid/unpaid transfer arrangements and platform-level paths.

HDB block counts are not residents. Master Plan zoning is not employment or footfall. The 800 m land-use summary uses parcel centroids and whole parcel areas, which can overstate nearby activity for large sites. Bus-stop locations do not show service frequency, capacity or transfer demand; the 400 m count is therefore descriptive and is not part of the uncalibrated station-choice utility. Straight-line distance ignores network topology and travel time. The OD file counts fare transactions between entry and exit points, not all passengers moving through an interchange. If the supplied OD month predates a current station, the station list and observed demand need to be reconciled before calibration.

The fixed-origin counterfactual can describe redistribution among existing travellers but will understate demand at newly opened stations. A full forecast would need future households, jobs, bus feeder changes, train travel times, operating dates, and induced trips. Coefficients estimated on today’s network may also change when the network changes. Until LTA’s actual OD file is supplied, none of the model’s numerical claims can be checked.

10 Conclusion

The geographic scenario adds 29 distinct station locations after interchange codes are reconciled. In the HDB building layer, 1,319 blocks cross the 800 m straight-line proximity threshold, with the largest groups near Pasir Ris East, Serangoon North, and Tengah Plantation. That is evidence of a possible access gain, not evidence of station ridership. The model, validation and future tap-out comparison are ready to run on an authorised LTA OD Train extract; their results remain open until that observed file is available.

## Geographic measures before ridership calibration

### Residential blocks within reach

I take the centroid of each completed HDB building polygon and find its nearest existing and proposed station. An 800 m threshold is a simple spatial screen: it asks whether a block's mapped centre lies within 800 m in a straight line. The count is not a population estimate, because blocks differ in floor count and household size. It also does not measure an actual walking route.

```{r}
#| label: coverage-counts
knitr::kable(coverage[4:6, ], col.names = c("Measure", "HDB blocks"))
```

Of 13,436 buildings, 9,645 are within 800 m of an existing physical station. The scenario adds 1,319 buildings to that threshold. A further 2,110 buildings are nearer to a proposed station than to any current one, whether or not they cross the 800 m line. These two figures answer different questions: new threshold coverage versus a shorter straight-line distance.

```{r}
#| label: coverage-map
knitr::include_graphics("figures/hdb-new-coverage.png")
```

The newly covered blocks are concentrated around planned stops in the west and north-east. The west contains much of the JRL extension's residential catchment, while the eastern CRL1 stations add pockets around Pasir Ris East and Tampines North. This map is a *geographic opportunity* measure, not a forecast of journeys: some blocks may already reach rail by bus, and an apparently close station may require a longer walk around barriers.

```{r}
#| label: line-coverage
knitr::kable(line_coverage,
             col.names = c("Nearest proposed line", "Newly reached HDB blocks"))
```

The line totals assign each newly reached building to its closest new station. They should not be read as a benefit–cost comparison of the two projects: the lines serve different places, and HDB buildings exclude private housing and many work destinations.

```{r}
#| label: new-blocks-chart
knitr::include_graphics("figures/new-station-blocks.png")
```

Pasir Ris East has the largest count in this measure (216), followed by Serangoon North (151) and Tengah Plantation (144). The chart assigns each newly reached block to its nearest proposed station, so a block is counted once. It does not imply that these will be the busiest new stations. Business districts and interchange stations can draw riders from much farther away than the surrounding HDB blocks.

### Sensitivity to the threshold

```{r}
#| label: threshold-check
knitr::kable(sensitivity, col.names = c("Radius (m)", "Existing blocks reached", "Newly reached blocks"))
```

The 800 m result is not a natural boundary. The table repeats the same centroid calculation at 600 m and 1,000 m. A larger radius includes more buildings but also accepts walks that may be unattractive or impossible in practice. The model itself uses continuous station-to-station distance rather than treating these circles as a rigid passenger market.

### Destination activity proxy

For each station, I count HDB block centroids and sum the area of mapped commercial, business, civic, education, health, hotel and mixed-use parcels whose centroids fall within 800 m. The land-use layer records **zoning**, not occupied jobs or realised visits. A large parcel whose centre lies just inside the circle is counted in full, so the figure is an approximate activity proxy. The two measures are kept separate in the model: one describes nearby housing blocks; the other describes mapped non-residential opportunities.

```{r}
#| label: activity-chart
knitr::include_graphics("figures/proposed-activity.png")
```

The activity ranking differs from the HDB-block ranking. That is the reason to include both predictors: a station serving industrial or commercial land could attract destination trips even with few completed HDB blocks nearby. The chart does not tell us how many workers or visitors use those parcels.

```{r}
#| label: activity-preview
preview <- features |>
  dplyr::filter(status == "Planned new") |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(activity_hectares_800m)) |>
  dplyr::select(station, hdb_blocks_800m, activity_hectares_800m) |>
  head(8)
knitr::kable(preview, digits = 1,
             col.names = c("Proposed station", "HDB blocks (800 m)", "Activity land (ha, approximate)"))
```

### Nearby bus stops

The LTA bus-stop layer has 5,205 unique stop codes. For each of the 29 new physical station locations, I count mapped stop poles within 400 m of the station point. This is a different check from the 800 m HDB building screen: it describes nearby bus infrastructure, not the number of residents or a catchment of passengers.

```{r}
#| label: bus-stop-chart
knitr::include_graphics("figures/proposed-bus-stops.png")
```

Choa Chu Kang West has 16 mapped stops within 400 m; Pandan Reservoir and Serangoon North have 14 each. The [complete station table](https://github.com/davincuaso/ISSS608-VAA/blob/master/Take-home_Ex/Take-home_Ex03/results/new-station-bus-stops.csv) includes all 29 locations. These counts cannot distinguish a busy transfer point from a group of lightly served roadside stops. Routes, headways, stop direction and walking connections would be needed before treating bus access as a behavioural predictor.

## Interaction data and observed market potential

The model script constructs a full directed choice table rather than using only pairs that appear in the OD CSV. Zero-flow pairs must remain in the choice set; otherwise the denominator in a station-choice probability would be calculated from observed trips alone. A same-station trip is removed because its zero spatial distance is not meaningful for this interstation model. Distances use station points in SVY21; they are **not** rail travel times or network path lengths.

```{r}
#| label: interaction-schema
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Table = c("Current interactions", "Proposed interactions", "Origins", "Destinations"),
  Key = c("origin + destination", "origin + destination", "origin", "destination"),
  Fields = c("observed trips, attraction, distance_km, probability",
             "attraction, distance_km, probability",
             "observed outbound weekday trips = market_potential",
             "observed inbound weekday trips, HDB blocks, activity area, line count")
), col.names = c("Data frame", "Join key", "Principal columns"))
```

LTA merges some interchange codes in the OD file (for example `CC1-NE6-NS24`). `R/model.R` splits these codes and maps their components to one physical station name. It saves unmatched codes and stops if they represent more than 5% of trip counts. The file must contain exactly one `YEAR_MONTH`, valid hourly values, and non-negative trips. Only `WEEKDAY` and `TRAIN` rows enter this version of the model. The origin total is a monthly aggregate across weekdays, not a per-day rate.

## Calibration and validation

For an origin *i* and available destination *j*, the station-choice utility is

$$
U_{ij}=\beta_H\log(1+H_j)+\beta_A\log(1+A_j)+\beta_L\log(L_j)-\beta_D\log(d_{ij}+0.25),
\qquad
P_{ij}=\frac{\exp(U_{ij})}{\sum_{k\ne i}\exp(U_{ik})}.
$$

Here $H_j$ is HDB block count within 800 m, $A_j$ is approximate activity hectares, $L_j$ is the number of rail lines, and $d_{ij}$ is straight-line distance in kilometres. The 0.25 km offset keeps the distance term finite at very short separations. The four coefficients are fitted by maximising the conditional multinomial likelihood of observed OD trips. The coefficient bounds enforce non-negative attraction effects and non-negative distance decay; a boundary estimate would warn that a predictor may add little information. These are modelling choices, not measured behavioural constants.

I reserve 20% of origin stations, selected with seed 626, before fitting. Their trip-weighted log loss is compared with a fitted distance-only model. The final coefficients are then refitted to all observed origins. For the current network, estimated destination tap-outs are the sum of each origin's observed market potential multiplied by its destination probabilities. The code checks that probabilities sum to one per origin and that total estimated trips equal the observed trip total.

```{r}
#| label: model-results
#| results: asis
if (has_model) {
  checks <- read.csv(file.path(model_dir, "checks.csv"))
  coefficients <- read.csv(file.path(model_dir, "coefficients.csv"))
  cat("The supplied OD file covers **", checks$month[1], "**. The model matched **",
      round(100 * checks$matched_trip_share[1], 1),
      "%** of weekday trips to the station coordinate table.\n\n", sep = "")
  print(knitr::kable(coefficients, digits = 3,
                     col.names = c("Model term", "Fitted coefficient")))
  cat("\nThe held-out log loss per trip is **", round(checks$heldout_logloss_per_trip[1], 3),
      "**, compared with **", round(checks$distance_only_logloss_per_trip[1], 3),
      "** for distance alone. The current-network station MAE is **",
      fmt(round(checks$station_mae[1])), "** monthly weekday tap-outs.\n", sep = "")
} else {
  cat("::: {.callout-warning title=\"Calibration pending\"}\n",
      "The LTA OD Train file has not been supplied. There are no fitted coefficients,",
      "validation scores or observed-versus-estimated station ridership values to report.\n:::\n")
}
```

## Proposed-network comparison

The first counterfactual holds each **existing origin's observed outbound trip total fixed** and adds the 29 distinct new station locations as possible destinations. Existing interchanges gain their proposed line connection. The fitted coefficients stay unchanged. This isolates a change in destination choice under the expanded set of stations. It does **not** estimate new trips generated by future housing, trips starting at new stations, or transfers inside paid rail areas. New-station figures from this scenario would be captured tap-outs from existing origins, not total future station ridership.

```{r}
#| label: scenario-results
#| results: asis
if (has_model) {
  pred <- read.csv(file.path(model_dir, "station-predictions.csv"))
  top_new <- pred |>
    dplyr::filter(status == "Planned new") |>
    dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(estimated_scenario)) |>
    dplyr::select(destination, estimated_scenario) |>
    head(10)
  print(knitr::kable(top_new, digits = 0,
                     col.names = c("New destination", "Captured monthly weekday tap-outs")))
  existing_change <- pred |>
    dplyr::filter(status == "Existing") |>
    dplyr::arrange(change) |>
    dplyr::select(destination, change, change_pct) |>
    head(10)
  cat("\nThe largest modelled reductions among existing destination stations are:\n\n")
  print(knitr::kable(existing_change, digits = 1,
                     col.names = c("Existing station", "Trip change", "Change (%)")))
} else {
  cat("The comparison table will be populated from the LTA OD file. No future-station",
      "ridership or existing-station share change is claimed yet.\n")
}
```

The interaction outputs retain `origin`, `destination`, `attraction`, `distance_km` and probability for both networks. They can be inspected directly rather than relying on a map's colour scale. Since the scenario conserves origin totals, gains at new destinations must be balanced by losses at existing destinations; this is a feature of this *fixed-market* scenario, not a statement that systemwide rail demand cannot grow.

## Assumptions and limitations

The coordinate file is a secondary compilation and may not place every platform or entrance exactly where passengers enter. The `JS2A` omission follows the brief's 24-code JRL scope rather than claiming the station is not planned. Station name grouping is suitable for physical locations, but it masks separate paid/unpaid transfer arrangements and platform-level paths.

HDB block counts are not residents. Master Plan zoning is not employment or footfall. The 800 m land-use summary uses parcel centroids and whole parcel areas, which can overstate nearby activity for large sites. Bus-stop locations do not show service frequency, capacity or transfer demand; the 400 m count is therefore descriptive and is not part of the uncalibrated station-choice utility. Straight-line distance ignores network topology and travel time. The OD file counts fare transactions between entry and exit points, not all passengers moving through an interchange. If the supplied OD month predates a current station, the station list and observed demand need to be reconciled before calibration.

The fixed-origin counterfactual can describe redistribution among existing travellers but will understate demand at newly opened stations. A full forecast would need future households, jobs, bus feeder changes, train travel times, operating dates, and induced trips. Coefficients estimated on today's network may also change when the network changes. Until LTA's actual OD file is supplied, none of the model's numerical claims can be checked.

## Conclusion

The geographic scenario adds 29 distinct station locations after interchange codes are reconciled. In the HDB building layer, 1,319 blocks cross the 800 m straight-line proximity threshold, with the largest groups near Pasir Ris East, Serangoon North, and Tengah Plantation. That is evidence of a possible access gain, not evidence of station ridership. The model, validation and future tap-out comparison are ready to run on an authorised LTA OD Train extract; their results remain open until that observed file is available.
